title: Poverty Point earthworks
summary: Poverty Point, in northeastern Louisiana, is a complex of earthen mounds, six semi-elliptical ridges with an outer diameter of 1.14 km, and a large plaza, built by hunter-fisher-gatherers in the Late Archaic period, between 3,700 and 3,100 years before present. Mound A, about 22 m high with a cross-shaped plan, is among the largest earthen mounds in North America.

uncertainty.note: The sources give 3,700 to 3,100 BP. Conversion to calendar years uses the usual 1950 datum for BP, which is not stated on the pages opened, so it is approximate (3,700 BP is about 1750 BCE, 3,100 BP about 1150 BCE). UNESCO's own text also writes the span as '3,700-3,100 years ago'.

as_recorded.value: in the main constructed 3,700-3,100 years ago in the Late Archaic period

importance.justification: UNESCO inscribed it in 2014 and calls it a singular achievement in earthen construction by hunter-fisher-gatherers, not surpassed in North America for at least 2,000 years.

phases.description: Mound A was built 3,400-3,100 BP, the largest and latest mound at Poverty Point (ICOMOS; BP converted to calendar years with the 1950 datum).
By 3,100 BP evidence of Late Archaic occupation falls and nothing similar reappears; only limited later occupation (ICOMOS). The mound survives, now mostly grass-covered.

reviewer_note: Shape mound: Mound A is the one structure modelled, with ICOMOS figures only (22 m high, 215 by 200 m). An older National Park Service survey form gives a mound 640 by 710 feet at the base and nearly 70 feet high, which is a different, older measurement and is not used. Dates are BP as given, converted with the 1950 datum, so the calendar years are approximate. The coordinate is UNESCO's property point (32°38'13"N 91°24'23"W, converted to decimal), within about 0.4 km of the OSM site point; neither is Mound A's own point, hence 1 km.
